connections.observation: s001 traces δόξα and δοκέω from fathers praising reputation (363a) through poets' teachings (364a) to the young man's calculus (365b–c) and Adeimantus' final demand (367b–c); s014 contrasts αὐτὸ δικαιοσύνην with τὰς ἀπʼ αὐτῆς εὐδοκιμήσεις at 363a and repeats the demand for what justice does αὐτὴ διʼ αὑτήν at 366e and 367d. Held together, these signals make visible a sustained configuration: reputation-language saturates every speaker's discourse (fathers, poets, the hypothetical young man, Adeimantus himself), yet the section's argumentative movement directs all this language toward isolating the αὐτό—what justice itself does—from the surrounding cloud of δόξα it has accumulated.

s002 shows πείθω shifting agents and objects across the section: begging priests persuade rich and gods (364b–c), poets must be believed or not (365e), the young man will persuade or compel (365d), and fathers should have persuaded the young (367a). s015 concentrates the mechanism of sacrifice (θυσίαι, ἐπῳδαί, εὐχωλαί, λοιβή, κνίση) at 364b–e, culminating in the young man's pairing ἀδικητέον καὶ θυτέον (365e). Together these make visible that persuasion becomes materially enacted through sacrifice: the gods themselves are persuaded (πείθοντες) to serve through θυσίαι (364c), and the entire logic of managing divine attention resolves into ritual practice.

s004 traces λανθάνω as the central practical problem: escaping notice of humans (365c–d), of gods (365d–e), finally appearing in Adeimantus' demand whether justice escapes notice or not (366e, 367e). s003 pairs persuasion and force (πείσομεν … βιασόμεθα at 365d) and notes δοκεῖν 'overpowers' truth (βιᾶται, 365c). The conjunction reveals that escaping notice structures the young man's entire plan: where he cannot persuade he will compel (365d), where gods cannot be escaped he shifts to whether they exist or can be bribed (365d–e), but the condition λανθάνειν governs each tactical decision, making it visible as the operational premise underlying the choice between persuasion and force.

s006 marks Hades appearing three times (363c, 363d, 366a); s008 contrasts eternal drunkenness (363d) with mud and sieve (363d); s016 pairs τελεταί and τελευτήσασιν at 365a and returns τελεταί as the answer to afterlife penalty (366a). Held together, Hades appears first as the site of divergent poetic afterlives (banquet versus futile labor), then as the place where penalty might be paid (366a), but immediately answered by τελεταί (366a) which already appeared alongside τελευτήσασιν (365a). The configuration makes visible that the vocabulary of completion (τελετή, τελευτάω) and the spatial site of afterlife judgment form an answering pair: initiation rites are positioned precisely to nullify the completed life's reckoning.

s007 concentrates concrete natural abundance in the Hesiod and Homer quotations (acorns, bees, sheep, wheat, barley, fruit, fish). s017 presents the young man's plan combining architectural facade (σκιαγραφία ἀρετῆς as πρόθυρα) with Archilochus' crafty fox (κερδαλέα καὶ ποικίλη) dragged behind. Together these make the difference between poetic and calculated imagery visible: the poets pile concrete, growth-generating goods as divine gifts for justice; the young man's response is a two-layered construction—painted surface in front, animal cunning concealed behind—that replaces agricultural generation with architectural and animal deception.

s009 sets the Hesiod quotation's two roads side by side: vice has a smooth, nearby path; virtue has a long, rough, uphill road preceded by sweat. s017 describes the young man drawing a painted facade of virtue in a circle around himself (σκιαγραφίαν ἀρετῆς περιγραπτέον) while dragging the fox behind. Held together, these reveal the young man has answered the two-roads image with a spatial reversal: instead of choosing one road or the other, he surrounds himself with virtue's appearance (the encircling σκιαγραφία) while the actual direction of travel is defined by what he drags behind (the fox ἐξόπισθεν), collapsing the choice between roads into a simultaneous occupation of contradictory spatial positions.

s012 traces ἐπαινέω: others praise justice but only for consequences (362e, 363a), no one has praised justice itself (366e), Adeimantus commands Socrates to praise it for what it does in the soul (367d). s014 contrasts αὐτὸ δικαιοσύνην (363a) with its external reputational effects and demands examination of what each does αὐτὴ διʼ αὑτήν (366e, 367d). Together these make visible that the entire section is staged as a problem about praise: every cited speaker praises, but the form of their praise (directed at consequences) makes it not-yet-praise of the thing itself, and Adeimantus' final demand to Socrates is for a different εἶδος of praise (367d: ἐπαίνεσον) directed at the isolated αὐτό.

s010 notes Socrates names Adeimantus as Glaucon's ἀδελφός and immediately invokes the proverb ἀδελφὸς ἀνδρὰ παρείη, applying the term to both literal and proverbial relation. s018 records Adeimantus announcing the most essential point (ὃ μάλιστα ἔδει ῥηθῆναι) has not been stated and that he will supply what Glaucon ἐλλείπει. Held together, these make visible that the section opens with Socrates invoking the proverb to authorize Adeimantus' assistance, and Adeimantus immediately performs the proverbial role by identifying and supplying the lack in his brother's argument, enacting the proverb as the structure of the speech itself.

s013 names six poets as authorities: Hesiod, Homer, Musaeus, Pindar, Archilochus, Orpheus. s002 shows πείθω shifting through begging priests persuading rich and gods (364b–c), poets who must be believed (365e), and fathers who should have persuaded the young (367a). Held together, the six named poets appear in three distinct rhetorical positions: Hesiod and Homer are cited by fathers as testimony (363a–c), Musaeus and Orpheus are invoked by begging priests to persuade cities and individuals (364e–365a), Pindar and Archilochus are quoted by the hypothetical young man in his internal deliberation (365b–c). The distribution makes visible that poetic authority is not monolithic but dispersed across different persuasive situations, each adapting cited verse to its context.

s019 contrasts mutual external surveillance (ἀλλήλους ἐφυλάττομεν) with each being his own best guardian (αὐτὸς αὑτοῦ … ἄριστος φύλαξ) in a counterfactual about proper praise. s001 shows δόξα saturating every discourse level. Together these make visible that guarding and reputation are inversely related in Adeimantus' counterfactual: if justice had been praised for what it does in the soul from childhood, each would guard himself (internal, reflexive φύλαξ), not watch others; but because it was praised for δόξα, guarding becomes mutual and external (ἀλλήλους), suggesting that praise directed at reputation produces a community structured by surveillance rather than self-governance.

s020 marks the pair ζῶντες / τελευτήσαντες appearing twice: purifications avail both (365a), and the unjust with facade succeeds both living and dead (366b). s006 shows Hades appearing three times as different sites (banquet 363c, mud 363d, penalty 366a). Held together, these reveal that the living/dead pair brackets the entire afterlife discourse: it opens the description of τελεταί (365a), reappears as the scope of success for the completely unjust life (366b), and the repeated pairing makes visible that every claim about divine reward or punishment must specify its temporal reach—whether it applies ἔτι ζῶσιν or after τελευτήσασιν—forcing the arguments to declare their jurisdiction across the boundary of death.

s005 shows μισθός appearing for poetic rewards (363d, twice) and returning in Adeimantus' demand to set aside μισθούς and δόξας (367d). s014 contrasts αὐτὸ δικαιοσύνην (363a) with external consequences and demands what justice does αὐτὴ διʼ αὑτήν (366e, 367d). Together these make visible that μισθός and δόξα are paired as the two categories to be subtracted (ἀφαίρει 367b, πάρες 367d): reputation (δόξα) is what fathers praise instead of justice itself (363a), rewards (μισθοί) are what poets promise (363d), and Adeimantus' command is to remove both simultaneously in order to isolate the αὐτό, treating them as a coupled obstruction to the thing itself.

s011 notes Socrates uses a wrestling image (καταπαλαῖσαι) for argumentative defeat and being rendered unable (ἀδύνατον) to defend justice. s002 traces πείθω culminating in the young man's plan to persuade or compel (πείσομεν … βιασόμεθα, 365d). Held together, these make visible that the section opens with Socrates already 'wrestled down' by Glaucon's speech, unable to assist justice (362d), and the young man's calculus later pairs persuasion with force (365d) as tactical alternatives. The configuration reveals that force and inability appear at the section's frame and center: Socrates is made unable by argumentative force, the young man plans to use actual force where persuasion fails, making the relation between λόγος and βία a governing concern that appears in both agonistic speech and projected action.

s021 lists seeing, hearing, thinking, being healthy as goods valuable τῇ αὑτῶν φύσει rather than for reputation. s014 demands examination of what justice does αὐτὴ διʼ αὑτήν. Held together, these make the vocabulary of reflexive possession visible: the exemplary goods are valuable αὑτῶν (their own nature, 367d), justice must be praised for what it does αὑτήν (itself through itself, 367d, 367e), and Adeimantus earlier demanded what each does αὑτοῦ δυνάμει (its own power, 366e). The repeated reflexive construction establishes a grammatical form for the demanded isolation: the αὐτό is to be grasped αὑτοῦ, through a possessive relation to itself that excludes external attribution.

s022 names two exceptions to involuntary justice: divine nature (θεία φύσις) and acquired knowledge (ἐπιστήμη, 366c–d). s019 presents the counterfactual that if justice had been praised correctly from youth, each would be his own best guardian (αὐτὸς αὑτοῦ … ἄριστος φύλαξ, 367a). Held together, these make visible an implicit triad of causes for just action: divine nature (θεία φύσις) and knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) are named as actual exceptions, but the counterfactual introduces a third—proper praise from childhood (ἐκ νέων ἡμᾶς ἐπείθετε, 367a)—which would produce self-guarding. The configuration reveals that Adeimantus is implicitly claiming that correct λόγος from youth could achieve what now requires either divine gift or acquired knowledge, positioning persuasive speech as a potential substitute for the two named exceptions.

elements.context: λέγουσι δέ που καὶ παρακελεύονται πατέρες τε ὑέσιν
τί οἰόμεθα ἀκουούσας νέων ψυχὰς ποιεῖν
παῖδας γὰρ παίδων φασὶ καὶ γένος κατόπισθεν λείπεσθαι

new_signals.observation: Generational vocabulary recurs: fathers address sons (πατέρες ... ὑέσιν, 362e), the souls of the young hear (νέων ψυχάς, 365a), proper persuasion should occur ἐκ νέων (367a), and descendants appear twice as παῖδες παίδων (363d, 366a). The concentration makes visible that the section is framed as speech directed across generations, from fathers to sons, affecting the young, with consequences extending to descendants.

elements.context: ὦ θαυμάσιε, πάντων ὑμῶν, ὅσοι ἐπαινέται φατὲ δικαιοσύνης εἶναι
ἀπὸ τῶν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἡρώων ἀρξάμενοι
οὐδεὶς πώποτε ἔψεξεν ἀδικίαν οὐδʼ ἐπῄνεσεν δικαιοσύνην ἄλλως

new_signals.observation: Adeimantus constructs a temporal sweep from the first heroes (ἀπὸ τῶν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἡρώων) to present humans (μέχρι τῶν νῦν ἀνθρώπων), asserting that no one ever (οὐδεὶς πώποτε) has praised justice correctly, addressing all who claim to be praisers (πάντων ὑμῶν ... ἐπαινέται). The construction makes visible that Adeimantus positions his indictment as total—spanning all time, all persons, all existing λόγοι—creating a universal absence against which he demands Socrates' speech.
